meta.title: F3: a Prairie Town home's year of energy by service and carrier, its useful energy, and a heat pump on a cold day
meta.note: The Prairie Town home is illustrative: it is built from real survey averages (EIA RECS 2020, West North Central census division, which includes Kansas), one typical car (EPA, 2022 data) and illustrative equipment efficiencies. The cold-day heat need and the heat pump's COP curve are an illustrative model, set to pass through a published DOE target. Every sourced number below carries its table or page and the date it was read.

heatpump.about: Illustrative model of a cold-climate air-source heat pump, not a device calculation: at or above the compressor cut-out, COP = 144 ÷ (45 − T) with T the day's outdoor average in °C, a curve chosen to give COP 2.4 at −15 °C, DOE's challenge target (2.4 × 60 = 144). Below the cut-out (−23 °C, the challenge's highest allowed cut-out) the compressor stops and a backup resistance heater runs at COP 1. The seasonal COP for the year is the challenge's HSPF2 of 8.5 Btu of heat per Wh of electricity ÷ 3.412.

day.about: Illustrative: on a day whose average outdoor temperature is T, the home needs 5 kWh of heat for each °C that T is below 18 °C.

bins.label: Device
bins.sub: what turns it into the service

cards.text: A warm room on a cold evening
cards.why: Nobody wants gas for its own sake: they want the warm room.
Gas carries chemical energy to the home through a pipe.
The service is hot water at the tap, whatever heats it.
Electricity carries energy from power plants through the wires.
It burns gas and turns its energy into heat for the rooms.
Travel is the service; a car, a bus or a bike can deliver it.
Gasoline carries chemical energy in the car's tank.
It uses electricity to move heat from outdoors into the house.
The fridge is the device; cold food is the service.

predict.q: In this home, which service takes the most energy in a year?

guess.q: Of the energy in the car's gasoline, what share actually moves the car?

apply.q: On a mild day a heat pump runs at a COP of 3.0 and delivers 90 kWh of heat. How many kWh of electricity did it use?
apply.why: Electricity = heat ÷ COP = 90 ÷ 3.0 = 30 kWh. The other 60 kWh came from the outdoor air.
